# Preface {.unnumbered}

Welcome to MATH7432, *Computing and Algorithms for Statistics*: a Master's module at
Lancaster University about the computational machinery that makes modern statistics run.
Statistics on paper is elegant; statistics in practice is code. This module teaches you to
write that code well, and to understand the algorithms it implements. Everything is in
both R and Python.

Every code chunk in these notes appears twice, side by side: **R on the left, Python on the right**, translated line for line. You are expected to **learn both languages**. R is the lingua franca of statistics, Python of
machine learning and production data science, and the modern statistician needs both in
their toolset! Working statisticians cross between the two languages constantly, and the side-by-side layout
teaches you to make that hop. One practical consequence: the side-by-side layout needs horizontal room, so read the notes on a wide screen (to be fair, it can work on a phone on a single column layout, but it kinda misses the point, and you probably want your phone for doomscrolling rather then reading the notes).

## Overview {.unnumbered}

The module will follow:

- **Weeks 1–4: Programming in R and Python** (each week: 1h lecture + 2h lab). We start
  from zero and build up both languages: variables, vectors and matrices (@sec-week1); logic, loops
  and iteration (@sec-week2); functions and functional programming (@sec-week3); data
  frames and plotting (@sec-week4). A running example threads through these weeks:
  **gradient descent**, the workhorse optimiser behind half of modern statistics and
  essentially all of machine learning. It appears in week 2 as a humble loop and grows up
  alongside your programming skills.

- **Week 5: Optimisation for statistics** (2h lecture + 1h lab). The payoff chapter,
  where the programming tools meet the statistics: estimation as loss minimisation,
  stochastic gradient descent, preconditioning, and quasi-Newton methods
  (BFGS); see @sec-week5.

**These notes cover weeks 1–5** The materials for weeks 6-10 will be released separately later in term, and will roughly cover the following topics:

- **Weeks 6–7: The bootstrap.** Nonparametric, parametric and semi-parametric
  bootstraps; standard errors, confidence intervals, and bias correction. Week 6 also
  hosts the **in-class test**.

- **Weeks 8–10: Markov chain Monte Carlo.** Random-walk Metropolis,
  Metropolis–Hastings, Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, convergence diagnostics, and Gibbs
  sampling.


## How to use these notes {.unnumbered}

The intended workflow:

- **Before the lecture:** skim the week's chapter. You don't need to understand everything: the lecture will give you the overview and the why.
- **During the lecture:** follow along, ask questions. You can take notes, but I will cover the same materials I have in these documents, so you don't need to copy everything down. 
- **In the lab:** work through the chapter at your own pace, copy-pasting the code into RStudio and running it yourself. Change things. Break things. Exercises
  appear throughout each chapter exactly where the relevant idea is fresh: do them as
  you meet them! If you get stuck, ask one of us for help.
- **Which language for the exercises?** Since you are building both, use the exercises to train the weaker one. If you already know one of the two languages, do the exercises in
  the other; if you know neither, alternate languages across the exercises. In every case, check the solutions for both languages.
- **Afterwards:** worked solutions are released on Moodle once all of the week's labs have ended.

Code you are meant to run appears in grey boxes; its output appears just below.

## Prerequisites {.unnumbered}

You might find that the rate of learning is faster than you expect. Well, it is. Since this is a Master's module, to proceed at the required speed we kind-of assume that you have: 

- **A good grasp of year 1 mathematics**. We will use calculus and linear algebra concepts (gradients, matrices, eigenvalues). Most of you from Lancaster will have covered these, but if you haven't you need to catch up. If you don't understand part of the maths, please ask as soon as possible.

- **Knowledge of basic statistics and probability**. We will use concepts such as random variables, distributions, and likelihoods. Again, as above, if you are not familiar with these, please get in touch.

- **Programming**. Most importantly, we assume that you have **some** programming experience. Many of you will have done some programming at some point, but if you haven't, don't worry: the first four weeks start from zero, however they progress quickly. If you have programmed before, the early weeks will be quick revision (although, if you have never never programmed before, please get in touch, so we can make sure you are not left behind).

## Sources {.unnumbered}

These notes build on, and reuse material from, two earlier Lancaster modules:

- Gaetano Romano and Eduard Campillo-Funollet, *MATH245 Computational Mathematics*,
  Lancaster University (also the source of the side-by-side R/Python format). 
- *MATH550/SCC.461 R Programming* (Statistics in Practice / Programming for Data
  Scientists), Lancaster University,
  <https://www.lancaster.ac.uk/~romano/teaching/2324MATH550/>.

This sets of notes essentially descends from the lineage of Debbie Costain, Clement Lee, Chris Nemeth, Tom Palmer, Florian Pein, Eduard Campillo-Funollet, Gaetano Romano and Stuart Sharples. I hope I haven't missed anyone (and if I have, please let me know).

For going deeper into R than we do here, the canonical further reading is
Hadley Wickham, *Advanced R*, 2nd edition, <https://adv-r.hadley.nz/>: free online, and
the source of several ideas and examples in these notes.

Right then. Open RStudio (which, as week 1 explains, speaks both of our languages) and
let's begin with @sec-week1.
